ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Committed to Collective Security, Says Brigadier General Adamneh - ENA English
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Committed to Collective Security, Says Major General Adamneh - ENA English - ENA Skip to Content Ethiopia Committed to Collective Security, Says Major General Adamneh - ENA English Live: አማርኛ ትግርኛ Afaan Oromoo Af‑Soomaali Qafar Afa English Français عربي Politics Social Economy Sport Technology Environment Feature Videos About Us Ethiopia Committed to Collective Security, Says Major General Adamneh 🔇Unmute Addis Ababa, November 10, 2026 (ENA)— Ethiopia remains committed to collective security with professionalism, discipline and sacrifice, Defense Peacekeeping Center Head Major General Adamneh Mengiste said. Speaking at the International Partners Day marked at the Defense Peacekeeping Center in Addis Ababa today, the head noted that Ethiopia’s contributions to global peace span decades beginning with the Korean War in 1951 and extending through missions in the Congo, Rwanda, Liberia, Burundi, Darfur, Abyei, South Sudan, and Somalia. The nation’s long history of peacekeeping is rooted in professionalism, discipline, and profound sacrifice, Major General Adamneh stated, reaffirming Ethiopia’s continued commitment to foster global peace and security. Underscoring the nation's deep-rooted role in collective security as a founding member of the United Nations and the African Union, the Center Head paid tribute to the peacekeepers that lost their lives in the line of duty. He recalled that 4 personnel tragically lost their lives in South Sudan in 2026 alone. "Their ultimate sacrifice will forever be etched in the history of our shared journey," Major General Adamneh stated. Commandant of the International Peace Support Training Institute (IPSTI), Brigadier General Gezahegn Fikadu noted the institute’s expanding role as an African center of excellence. The institute equips military, police, and civilian personnel for complex UN, EU, and regional operations through generic, specialized, and mission-specific training, he said. "IPSTI aspires to serve as an important platform for translating Ethiopia's wealth of practical experience into professional knowledge, skills, research, and training opportunities for the wider African and international peace support community." Noting that modern peace support operations demand deepened collaboration, shared technology, and sustainable institutional backing, Brigadier General Gezahegn emphasized the need for strengthening local and international partners to collaborate on joint training, research, logistical support, and regional standby force development. Major General Teshome Gemechu, Main Directorate Director of Defense International Relations and Military Cooperation at the Ministry of Defense, for his part emphasized the need to renew spirit of partnership to secure a more peaceful and stable future for Africa and the world. Enhanced partnership provides a strong foundation for continued operations, he stated, calling on partners to maintain the spirit of cooperation by working together, sharing new knowledge, and helping each other in different modalities. The International Partners Day was marked along with partners, including military attaches of various countries and representatives of international organizations under the theme “Invest in Peace: Building Resilient Partnerships for Global Security”. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden
ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia's commitment to collective security was emphasized by Major General Adamneh Mengiste during the International Partners Day at the Defense Peacekeeping Center in Addis Ababa. He highlighted Ethiopia's extensive history in peacekeeping, which dates back to the Korean War in 1951 and includes missions in various conflict zones such as South Sudan and Somalia. Major General Adamneh reaffirmed the nation’s dedication to global peace, rooted in professionalism and sacrifice, while honoring peacekeepers who lost their lives, including four personnel in South Sudan in 2026. Brigadier General Gezahegn Fikadu discussed the role of the International Peace Support Training Institute (IPSTI) in enhancing military and civilian training for peace operations. He stressed the importance of collaboration and shared resources among local and international partners to strengthen peace efforts. Major General Teshome Gemechu called for renewed partnerships to ensure a stable future for Africa and the world, aligning with the theme of the event: “Invest in Peace: Building Resilient Partnerships for Global Security.”

ethiopia.content: Kenya monitoring security situation as Ethiopian refugees flock Moyale For You News Faida Cafe Watch Radio TV Podcasts Live Events Search Kenya monitoring security situation as Ethiopian refugees flock Moyale By Terry Karanja November 10, 2026 03:14 (EAT) Add as a Preferred Source on Google Follow us Follow on Whatsapp Follow on Google Follow on Twitter Interior PS Raymond Omollo chairing the Fifth Programme Steering Committee meeting and official launch of the Resilient Livelihoods, Vulnerable Youth and Communities Empowerment Initiative on Thursday, August 13, 2026. PHOTO | COURTESY Audio By Vocalize Principal Secretary for the State Department for Internal Security and National Administration Raymond Omollo has said Kenya is monitoring increased security risks as Ethiopian refugees flock Moyale. Omollo said on Tuesday that refugees coming to the country had put the security sector under pressure. “This security situation, where different groups are fighting, we've had cases of stray bullets coming into the Kenyan side,” Omollo told NTV. “The Inspector General of police was there at the end of last week together with a team from the national government administration just to calm the situation and manage it." The PS argued that an increase in population of refugees can lead to disease outbreak thus working towards having enough medical supplies. “We are looking at medical supplies, particularly to address the issues around disease outbreak if it gets to that point,” he added. He also confirmed the continued security monitoring by having active conversations between Kenyan and Ethiopian officials. “Most importantly is community engagement and sensitization so that then even as there is escalation or movement, then we don't have the locals feeling like they are being pushed to act so that then we have retaliation or something like that,” he insisted. Omollo added that Moyale leaders had also been engaged in these conversations. ethiopia.title: Ethiopian Americans Are Gaining Political Ground: Is Ethiopia’s Policy Keeping Up? - horn review
ethiopia.content: Ethiopian Americans Are Gaining Political Ground: Is Ethiopia’s Policy Keeping Up? – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-11-10 Ethiopian Americans Are Gaining Political Ground: Is Ethiopia’s Policy Keeping Up? 0 Comments For Ethiopia, the diaspora represents both a political challenge and a largely underutilized strategic asset. Its influence extends from domestic political dynamics and armed movements to the political institutions and policymaking circles of its host countries. Its involvement in Ethiopian affairs has taken various forms, with sections of the diaspora, particularly opposition groups, seeking to influence domestic political developments while lobbying their host governments to exert pressure on Addis Ababa over issues ranging from human rights to broader governance concerns. These efforts have also been directed at the United States, home to hundreds of thousands of Ethiopians in the diaspora. For many years, however, their attempts to influence Washington’s policy toward Ethiopia have had limited success , because the United States has continued to give greater weight to its security cooperation with Addis Ababa, especially in addressing terrorism and instability in the Horn of Africa. In conceptual terms, the Ethiopian diaspora relatively fits Lyons’ notion of a “conflict-generated diaspora”, formed by people displaced by violence, conflict and political repression, whose ties to their homeland remain deeply shaped by memories of trauma and displacement. Because of this its influence extends beyond financial support to families and communities back home. Diaspora remittances can also sustain political or armed groups, while diaspora communities can shape political debates, influence party strategies and strengthen the legitimacy of political leaders. Conflict generated diasporas can therefore affect the course of conflicts through their financial resources, political networks and capacity to shape narratives, all of which can alter local conflict dynamics. The effects of such a diaspora also extend to second and later generations. Although these generations did not experience the original conflicts directly, they may inherit their families’ memories, political grievances and emotional attachments to the homeland, and these inherited experiences can continue to shape their perceptions of Ethiopia and their engagement with its politics. The recent election of Ethiopian-born Melat Kiros to the US Congress illustrates how subsequent generations can retain political connections to their ancestral homeland. Despite having moved to the United States as an infant, Melat has maintained an attachment to her Tigrayan heritage and has publicly drawn on the experiences of conflict in northern Ethiopia in explaining her political activism. Her case illustrates how memories of homeland conflicts can be transmitted across generations and continue to shape political engagement in the countries where diaspora communities settle. On the other hand, some young Ethiopian Americans have increasingly embraced a broader “Habesha” identity. They drew on Ethiopia’s historical heritage, cultural traditions and past achievements to strengthen their sense of connection to their ancestral homeland. A particularly relevant example is Illinois State Senator Mike Simmons, the son of an Ethiopian refugee and the first Ethiopian American to serve in the Illinois Senate. In March 2025, he formally recognized March 2 as Adwa Day, celebrating Ethiopia’s 1896 victory over Italian colonial forces. Describing himself as a “proud Habesha,” Simmons used his position in the Illinois legislature to recognize Ethiopia’s historical heritage and acknowledge the sizeable Ethiopian communities in his constituency. Although the Ethiopian diaspora has achieved limited success in influencing US policy toward Ethiopia, its political influence and potential is should not be underestimated. The diaspora’s ability to mobilize, shape public debate and engage political representatives in their host countries can create opportunities to influence policy over time. In the US, Ethiopian diaspora groups organized demonstrations in various US cities, contacted members of Congress, submitted appeals to the State Department and sought to influence congressional discussions on Ethiopia. The developments mentioned above show that the diaspora’s contribution to Ethiopia can extend well beyond remittances and financial investment. Its growing presence in political institutions abroad offers opportunities to strengthen Ethiopia’s international visibility, cultural diplomacy and access to foreign policymaking circles. The Ethiopian government should recognize this potential and approach the diaspora as a strategic partner, establishing sustained relationships with Ethiopian-origin politicians, professionals, academics and community leaders. Such engagement should not be limited to individuals already active in Ethiopian affairs. It should also identify and build relationships with emerging political figures and potential candidates of Ethiopian heritage across different states and levels of government in the United States, creating connections before they reach positions of greater political influence. A broader engagement strategy could also help address the domestic consequences of diaspora involvement in Ethiopia’s conflicts. Financial contributions, political advocacy and media mobilization from abroad have in some cases supported actors engaged in domestic political and armed struggles. By addressing the grievances that encourage such involvement and by providing credible channels for political participation, the government could reduce the appeal of armed mobilization and limit the financial and political support available to insurgent movements. The 2005 general elections illustrate how significant this involvement can be, as they marked an important turning point in the diaspora’s direct role in domestic politics. Ethiopians living abroad supported opposition parties, raised funds, shaped political debates and helped build alliances among political groups, and some activists even returned to Ethiopia to take part directly in electoral politics. Moreover, one of the principal challenges within the diaspora is its fragmentation along ethnic and identity-based lines. This fault line has been further deepened by successive Ethiopian governments’ failures to establish sustained and inclusive engagement with diaspora communities, often approaching their political activism with suspicion and viewing it as a challenge to domestic authority. This might make engagement difficult, particularly when government outreach is perceived as favoring one community or political constituency over another. The government must therefore adopt an inclusive and accommodating approach, recognizing the diversity of diaspora experiences and political positions. It should be prepared to engage with groups and individuals whose views differ from its own, including critics of government policy. In 2024, the government launched a “back to your origins” initiative that invited second generation members of the diaspora from North America, Europe and elsewhere to visit Ethiopia and learn about their heritage, historical roots and identity. Initiatives of this kind remain important for strengthening relations between the government and diaspora communities, and they should be encouraged and institutionalized. More broadly, the government needs a coherent approach that moves beyond remittances and recognizes the diaspora’s political, economic and intellectual potential. This approach should include deliberate efforts to reach second and later generations, many of whom have limited direct ties to the country, and to strengthen their sense of belonging and engagement with Ethiopia. Policy toward the diaspora in the United States should accordingly treat it as a strategic partner in development, public diplomacy, foreign policy advocacy, bilateral relations and the advancement of Ethiopia’s national interests. It should prioritize trust-building, rights expansion, targeted economic instruments, skills circuits, and constructive political engagement. Translating these policy priorities into practice requires the government to engage with the diaspora through the existing community networks and institutions that shape its social and political activities. Ethiopian diaspora associations often begin by bringing people together around shared cultural, professional and community interests, but the networks they establish can also facilitate wider political mobilization. For example, Ethiopian community associations, religious institutions and professional networks in the United States provide spaces for social interaction, information exchange and collective organization. During periods of political crisis in Ethiopia, these established connections can help mobilize people for demonstrations, fundraising campaigns and advocacy initiatives. An example is the American Ethiopian Public Affairs Committee (AEPAC), established in 2021 to organize Ethiopian Americans around advocacy for stronger US–Ethiopia relations. Through congressional engagement, political fundraising, voter mobilization and outreach to US policymakers, the organization demonstrates how diaspora networks can develop into structured platforms for influencing foreign policy and political debate. At the same time, engagement with various institutions requires careful consideration of their internal political dynamics to ensure that they do not become platforms for partisan competition, identity-based polarization or the mobilization of support for armed movements. The 2026 US midterm elections provide a recent illustration of this political potential. The Trump administration faced a major electoral setback, with Democrats winning control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. The elections also brought several politicians of African origin or heritage into elected office at both federal and state levels. One notable illustration is the growing political representation of Americans of Ethiopian heritage in the United States. Several individuals with Ethiopian roots have secured elected and appointed positions, including seats in legislative institutions, demonstrating the diaspora’s expanding presence in American political life. The growing presence of Ethiopian-origin Americans in US political institutions is also reflected in the careers of Melat Kiros, Samra Brouk, Mike Simmons, Girmay Zahilay, Amsalu Kassaw, Oballa Oballa, Alexander Assefa, Yema T. Measho and Nina Ashenafi-Richardson. Their political trajectories span the US Congress, state legislatures, county government, municipal councils and the judiciary. Melat’s election to the US House of Representatives in Colorado in the recent election is particularly notable, while Samra retained her New York State Senate seat. Their representation, alongside the earlier political achievements of Simmons, Zahilay and others, illustrates the expanding institutional presence of Americans with Ethiopian roots. For the Ethiopian government, these developments reinforce the strategic importance of proactive engagement with both established and emerging Ethiopian-American political figures. Such outreach should seek to build relationships across the political spectrum, recognizing that these individuals may hold divergent views on Ethiopia’s domestic politics, foreign policy and bilateral relations. While some may become important partners in strengthening Ethiopia–US relations, others may adopt critical positions or advocate policies that challenge the government’s interests. A sustained and inclusive approach would help Ethiopia maintain channels of communication across these differing political orientations and avoid limiting its engagement to sympathetic voices. Therefore, a government that broadens its engagement with its diaspora stands to benefit in several ways. First, it can address the grievances and political frustrations that armed insurgent groups may exploit to mobilize diaspora support, limiting their ability to secure financial resources, political backing and international legitimacy. Second, sustained engagement can help build trust, encourage diaspora investment and remittances, and channel the diaspora’s political, intellectual and professional resources towards national development. In due course, meaningful diaspora engagement can help transform a constituency often viewed through the lens of political opposition and conflict into a constructive partner in Ethiopia’s political stability, national development and international engagement. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopian Americans are increasingly gaining political influence in the United States, presenting both opportunities and challenges for Ethiopia's government. The diaspora, often shaped by experiences of conflict and displacement, has sought to impact domestic political developments in Ethiopia while lobbying U.S. policymakers on issues like human rights. Despite limited success in influencing U.S. policy, the diaspora's ability to mobilize and engage politically is significant. Recent elections have seen Ethiopian Americans, such as Melat Kiros and Mike Simmons, secure political positions, highlighting the potential for future influence. However, the Ethiopian government has historically approached the diaspora with suspicion, often failing to engage inclusively. To leverage the diaspora's potential, Ethiopia should adopt a strategic partnership approach, recognizing the diverse experiences within the community and fostering connections with emerging political figures. Initiatives aimed at strengthening ties with younger generations of the diaspora are crucial for enhancing Ethiopia's international visibility and addressing domestic political challenges.

Two years later, with U.S. attention largely diverted to other areas of concern, we asked James to revisit his arguments.Image: Joseph Rullo via DVIDSIn your January 2024 piece, you warned that a memorandum of understanding signed between Ethiopia and Somaliland could actually accelerate al-Shabaab’s expansion into the two countries, pointing to its 2022 incursion into Ethiopia and its sleeper cells in cities like Hargeisa and Berbera. Has that threat materialized as you expected, and how has the group’s posture in both places changed since?The threat we described that al-Shabaab poses to Ethiopia and/or Somaliland has thankfully not yet materialized, although this is no guarantee against such an attack in the foreseeable future. Al-Shabaab is quite patient, and we were not wrong to highlight the evidence that it was building up networks in both countries. The best available evidence, plus my own discussions with Somali colleagues and contacts, indicates that al-Shabaab still maintains sophisticated networks across the region. Of course, when discussing covert cells and attack planning like this, we need to account for a good degree of uncertainty, but I don’t think everyone can breathe a sigh of relief just yet. Indeed, one dynamic we did not initially consider in our piece was how al-Shabaab’s growing ties to the Houthis could provide another vector for the group to attack or support an attack against either Ethiopia or Somaliland. somalia.summary: Two years after the Ethiopian-Somaliland deal, the threat of al-Shabaab's expansion remains a concern, although it has not yet materialized as predicted. In a 2024 analysis, James Barnett warned that the agreement could exacerbate tensions in the Horn of Africa, potentially leading to a broader conflict. While al-Shabaab has not launched significant attacks in Ethiopia or Somaliland, it continues to maintain sophisticated networks in the region. New dynamics, such as al-Shabaab's growing connections with the Houthis, could pose additional risks for both countries. As the U.S. focuses on other global issues, the situation remains precarious, and experts caution against complacency. The evolving landscape underscores the need for vigilance and strategic partnerships, particularly with Mogadishu, to counter the persistent threat of al-Shabaab. The analysis highlights the complexities of regional security and the potential for future instability if not addressed.

Somalia army faces waves of desertions as soldiers abandon frontlines following clan leader’s call November 10, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Somalia’s military is facing a potentially serious internal crisis after waves of soldiers from the Hawadle clan abandoned their positions in the national army and returned to Beledweyne, responding to a directive from their traditional leader, Ugas Yusuf Ugas Hassan, who called on Hawadle servicemen to withdraw from the frontlines and assemble at his residence. Footage circulating on social media shows dozens of Somali National Army (SNA) soldiers arriving at the clan leader’s residence in Beledweyne, the administrative capital of the Hiiraan region, following his appeal for members of the Hawadle clan serving in the military to abandon their positions and report to him. The residence has reportedly become a gathering point for returning soldiers, with successive groups arriving over the past two days. The mobilisation represents a potentially significant challenge to the federal government’s efforts to preserve military cohesion and maintain an integrated national force amid mounting political and clan-related tensions. The developments come at a particularly sensitive juncture for Somalia’s security transition. The country is working to assume greater responsibility for its national defence as African Union forces draw down their presence, while Ugandan troops operating under a separate bilateral security arrangement have also begun withdrawing. The apparent departures threaten to compound existing pressures on Somalia’s military establishment, raising questions about the reliability of frontline deployments, the unity of the army’s command structure and its capacity to sustain operations against Al-Shabaab. Hawadle leader signals possible military offensive Addressing soldiers who had returned to Beledweyne, Ugas Hassan reportedly said they would launch an offensive once sufficient numbers had assembled. He did not specify the intended target, outline an operational plan or clarify the circumstances under which the proposed military action would take place. His remarks have heightened concerns that the mobilisation could evolve beyond a symbolic demonstration of clan solidarity into a broader armed confrontation, particularly as relations between the Hawadle leadership and the federal government continue to deteriorate. The latest developments follow an earlier appeal by the traditional leader urging Hawadle clansmen to take up arms and defend Beledweyne against what he described as an impending offensive by rival clans allegedly operating under the protection of government forces. The allegations have not been independently established. Nevertheless, the rhetoric underscores the depth of the confrontation between the clan leadership and federal authorities, with the dispute increasingly taking on implications for the country’s wider security environment. Military withdrawals raise concerns over Al-Shabaab frontlines Of particular concern is the reported withdrawal of soldiers from strategically important military positions in Galgaduud, Lower Shabelle and Middle Shabelle, regions where government forces have been engaged in operations against Al-Shabaab. If confirmed, the departure of personnel from these areas could create operational vulnerabilities, weaken existing defensive positions and complicate efforts to sustain pressure on the militant group. The potential consequences extend beyond the immediate loss of manpower. Military deployments depend on coordination between units, continuity of command, intelligence-sharing arrangements and the ability to reinforce positions when security conditions deteriorate. Sudden departures could undermine these arrangements and place additional pressure on units remaining in the field. A breakdown in military cohesion could therefore provide Al-Shabaab with opportunities to exploit security gaps, particularly in areas where government forces are already operating under considerable logistical and operational constraints. Clan loyalties expose deeper challenges within Somalia’s national army Beyond its immediate military implications, the unfolding crisis highlights a longstanding structural challenge confronting Somalia: the difficulty of building a cohesive national army within a political and security environment where clan affiliations continue to exercise considerable influence. The apparent willingness of soldiers to respond to a traditional leader’s mobilisation appeal, even at the expense of their official military responsibilities, raises fundamental questions about the relationship between clan authority, institutional loyalty and the chain of command. For the federal government, the episode presents a particularly difficult test of its efforts to establish a unified military institution whose personnel remain accountable to national command structures rather than competing political or clan-based interests. A nationally representative army is central to Somalia’s long-term security strategy. Its effectiveness, however, depends not only on the composition of its ranks but also on the strength of its command arrangements, the discipline of its personnel and the institutional loyalties underpinning its operations. The growing confrontation between the Hawadle leadership and federal authorities threatens to expose vulnerabilities in all three areas. As tensions intensify in Beledweyne, the immediate concern is whether the returning soldiers will remain mobilised under clan leadership, whether the federal government can contain the dispute through political engagement, and what consequences their departure could have for military operations elsewhere. For a country attempting to reduce its dependence on foreign security forces while continuing its campaign against Al-Shabaab, a confrontation that draws national army personnel away from their assigned positions could hardly come at a more precarious moment. Somalia’s security transition now faces a challenge that extends beyond the battlefield: preserving the cohesion of the very military institution expected to safeguard the country’s future. somalia.summary: Somalia's military is experiencing a significant crisis as soldiers from the Hawadle clan abandon their posts in response to a call from their traditional leader, Ugas Yusuf Ugas Hassan. This mass withdrawal, which has seen numerous soldiers return to Beledweyne, poses a serious challenge to the federal government's efforts to maintain military cohesion amid rising political and clan tensions. The situation is particularly precarious as Somalia transitions to greater national defense responsibility while foreign troops withdraw. Ugas Hassan has indicated plans for a potential military offensive, raising fears of escalating conflict. The departures from key regions, such as Galgaduud and Lower Shabelle, could weaken defenses against Al-Shabaab, complicating ongoing military operations. This crisis underscores the difficulties of establishing a unified national army in a context where clan loyalties often supersede institutional allegiance, threatening the effectiveness and stability of Somalia's military forces at a critical juncture in its security landscape.

somalia.title: Suspected Al-Shabaab militants kill 8 in northeastern Kenya ambush - Anadolu Ajansı
somalia.content: Skip to main content Suspected Al-Shabaab militants kill 8 in northeastern Kenya ambush Reporting the Changing World CORPORATE History Executive Team Quality Management Editorial Guidelines Social Media Policies Logos Privacy and Cookies Policy Information Policy RSS Diary COMMUNICATION Contact Subscription Requests Anadolu Ajansı © 2026 WORLD TÜRKİYE ECONOMY POLITICS ENERGY TECHNOLOGY US-Iran war Hormuz crisis Russia-Ukraine war EDITION Türkçe English BHSC Pусский Français العربية Kurdî کوردی Shqip فارسی македонски Bahasa Indonesia Español Africa Suspected Al-Shabaab militants kill 8 in northeastern Kenya ambush 5 road workers, 2 police reservists, driver killed in attack near porous Somalia border Andrew Wasike 10 November 2026 • Update : 10 November 2026 NAIROBI, Kenya At least eight people, including five road construction workers and two police reservists, were killed Tuesday in a suspected Al-Shabaab ambush in Kenya's northeastern Mandera County, near the border with Somalia, according to media reports. The attackers opened fire on a vehicle escorting workers along the Arabia-Lafey road in the Hagarsu area, killing all eight occupants, including the driver. “It is particularly painful that individuals dedicated to advancing infrastructure and development in our county have lost their lives in such tragic circumstances,” Mandera Gov. Mohamed Adan Khalif said in a statement. Khalif urged an urgent investigation and the arrest of those responsible, saying residents deserved security and freedom from intimidation. Police deployed a multi-agency security team to pursue the attackers, while the bodies of the victims were taken to Mandera Teaching and Referral Hospital. The attack comes three days after suspected Al-Shabaab militants targeted police installations in neighboring Garissa County and attempted to attack a security base in Mandera. Security forces repelled the assaults. Mandera lies along Kenya's porous border with Somalia, where Al-Shabaab has waged an insurgency for nearly two decades. The al-Qaeda-linked group has repeatedly carried out attacks in northeastern Kenya, targeting security personnel, civilians and infrastructure projects. Kenya deployed troops to Somalia in 2011 to combat the militants, who have since launched deadly retaliatory attacks, including the deadly 2013 Westgate shopping mall siege in Nairobi and the 2015 Garissa University massacre. news_share news_share_description subscription_contact subscription contact_the_ombudsman is_there_an_error_in_this_story ombudsman_apply_button Previous Next Previous Turkish, Ethiopian leaders meet on sidelines of COP31 climate conference in Antalya Next 11 opposition parties back Burundi's president for 2027 election LATEST NEWS All Fire breaks out at Iran's South Pars gas platform Trump envoy Jared Kushner 'encouraged' by Russia-Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi US Republicans elect Jim Jordan as House minority leader Canada's prime minister to discuss 'non-interference' with China's Xi at Asia-Pacific summit Netanyahu, Trump reportedly clash over Iran in tense call: Report Member of US Army arrested in UK for suspected Russian espionage: Police Russian, Belarusian presidents meet ahead of security summit near Moscow See All
somalia.summary: Suspected Al-Shabaab militants ambushed a vehicle in northeastern Kenya's Mandera County on November 10, killing at least eight individuals, including five road construction workers, two police reservists, and the driver. The attack occurred near the Somalia border as the vehicle was escorting workers along the Arabia-Lafey road. Mandera Governor Mohamed Adan Khalif expressed deep sorrow over the loss of lives dedicated to infrastructure development and called for an urgent investigation to ensure the perpetrators are brought to justice. In response to the ambush, police have deployed a multi-agency security team to track down the attackers. This incident follows recent assaults by Al-Shabaab militants in neighboring Garissa County, highlighting the ongoing threat posed by the group, which has been active in the region for nearly two decades. Kenya has been combating Al-Shabaab since deploying troops to Somalia in 2011, facing numerous retaliatory attacks since then.

somalia.title: UN Women backs NUSOJ-led nationwide consultations on Somalia’s accession to CEDAW - Garowe Online
somalia.content: UN Women backs NUSOJ-led nationwide consultations on Somalia’s accession to CEDAW Latest Headlines UN Women backs NUSOJ-led nationwide consultations on Somalia’s accession to CEDAW Eight killed in suspected al-Shabaab ambush in northeast Kenya: police British-Somali boxer Ramla Ali wins first world titles at 37 after split-decision victory Tabaarak ICT’s Regional Award Marks Major Milestone for Somalia’s Technology Industry Former NISA chief challenges Hassan Sheikh's proposal to make Beledweyne Hirshabelle capital Advertise with us Home News Puntland Somalia World Sports Press Releases Somaliland Videos Opinion Contact Privacy Policy English Somali UN Women backs NUSOJ-led nationwide consultations on Somalia’s accession to CEDAW Press Release NUSOJ Posted On 10-11-2026, 05:56PM The National Union of Somali Journalists (NUSOJ) has launched a series of stakeholder consultations across Somalia to build public understanding and support for the country’s accession to the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW). The consultations opened in Mogadishu and are taking place across the country. They provide government institutions, civil society and community representatives with an opportunity to discuss the Convention, the accession process and its relevance to Somalia. Speaking at the opening, Acting Minister and State Minister for Family and Human Rights Development Mohamed Osman Omar said the consultations could help ensure that discussion on accession is informed and inclusive. “Somalia’s consideration of CEDAW calls for clear information and constructive engagement across society. These consultations provide an opportunity to discuss the Convention openly and consider how the accession process can support the protection of women’s rights in the Somali context,” he said. Rukaya Mohammed, Country Programme Manager of UN Women in Somalia, said dialogue could help communities and institutions understand the Convention and the steps involved in accession. “Informed dialogue helps communities and institutions understand what CEDAW means and how the accession process works. These consultations create space for questions, address misconceptions and bring different perspectives into the discussion, helping to advance the accession process,” she said. NUSOJ Secretary-General Omar Faruk Osman said the consultations would gather practical recommendations to inform the next steps. “The aim is to make sure people can engage with the issues, raise their concerns and contribute ideas. Their recommendations can help shape a roadmap that reflects Somalia’s realities and supports the country’s commitment to eliminate all forms of discrimination against women through accession to the Convention,” Osman said. The forums include presentations on CEDAW’s principles and accession procedures, followed by facilitated discussions and group work. Participants will consider questions and concerns in relation to Somalia’s constitutional framework, religious jurisprudence and customary values. NUSOJ is convening the consultations with support from UN Women and the Ministry of Family and Human Rights Development. The discussions aim to develop a set of recommendations for a roadmap to advance Somalia’s accession to CEDAW. Security Threats About ADF Contact Subscription Contribute Archive English Français العربية Português English Français العربية Português Home » Daily News » Renewed Somali Piracy Raises Concerns Daily News Renewed Somali Piracy Raises Concerns Attacks linked to Houthi rebels and illegal fishing, leaving local fishermen with empty nets By ADF November 10, 2026 4 Mins Read Puntland Maritime Police Forces conduct counter-piracy operations off the coast of Somalia. ANADOLU VIA GETTY IMAGES Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Email Reddit WhatsApp Copy Link An International Maritime Bureau piracy report noted a recent wave of Somali piracy incidents, which have surged since April. The pirates typically strike in the Gulf of Aden between Somalia and Yemen. While the overall number of Somali piracy incidents is down, analysts say the recent increase shows that the challenge persists. In the largest attack this year, Somali pirates on April 21 hijacked the Palau-flagged tanker Honour 25 near Eyl, a former fishing town in the autonomous Puntland region that has become a major hub of Somali piracy. Five crew members were killed and five injured during a rescue attempt in September. Analysts believe these marked the first killings committed by Somali pirates in more than 10 years. “While incident levels are at their lowest in more than three decades, the recent uptick in Somali piracy activity is a reminder that the threat remains,” Bureau Director Michael Howlett said in a defenceWeb report. “Incidents this year have also shown that strict adherence to BMP [Best Management Practices] recommendations remains one of the most effective ways to deter hijacking attempts and protect crews. Continued vigilance is essential to safeguarding seafarers and the vital trade routes on which the global economy depends.” The scourge is driven in part by Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels, whose attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz threaten shipping in the Red Sea and Indian Ocean, forcing companies to use lanes around the Horn of Africa. Multiple geopolitical crises in the region have also driven a reshuffling of naval assets, leaving Somali waters more exposed to sea crime. Increased piracy has coincided with the growing relationship between the Houthis and al-Shabaab, which has ties to Somali piracy. This has resulted in pirate groups using more sophisticated weaponry and technology acquired from the Houthis. Illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing aggravates the challenge. The fishing town of Bander Beyla, on the Puntland coast, has become a focal point of the renewed piracy crisis. Locals are struggling to make ends meet amid fishing restrictions and the presence of foreign fishing trawlers. Abdifatah Mohamed, who has spent 20 years fishing off Somalia’s coast, said the activities of foreign industrial trawlers have led to declining fish stocks. “We’re [fishermen] no match for the foreign trawlers, who possess capabilities far greater than us, which impacts the livelihoods of our families on land,” Mohamed told Al Jazeera. “Some from our community have taken up arms at sea, but deep down I know it’s hurting our community.” Local authorities in late August restricted fishermen from going to sea amid concerns that pirates were disguising themselves as fishermen; pirates often launch attacks from small dhows and seize fishing vessels, known as “mother ships.” “Some of the pirates involved in the hijackings are from Bander Bayla and hail from this community,” Abdirizak Said, a local fisherman, told Al Jazeera. He said dozens of locals have been arrested for bringing to pirates food or khat, a shrub chewed for its stimulant-like effect. “Businesses and stores were even ordered by the [local] government not to sell anything to pirates, and if they do, they’ll be viewed as pirates themselves,” Said told Al Jazeera. Locals say the fishing restriction, expected to last two months, fuels food and financial insecurity. “Our families depend on what we catch at sea,” Mohamed said. “Even though our catches have gone down in recent years, it helped provide for our families at home. But it’s like we were being punished for crimes we have nothing to do with, and our families have suffered for it.” According to the Soufan Center think tank, the resurgence in Somali piracy has not altered the international response, which focuses on deterrence. The center highlighted a new counter-piracy task force proposed by signatory countries of the Djibouti Code of Conduct (DCoC). The countries called for the creation of a regional task force to confront piracy and other crimes in the Gulf of Aden and the western Indian Ocean. The proposed DCoC Task Force was revealed on August 17 — a day when eight armed Somali pirates boarded the Cameroonian-flagged vessel MV Lutuf, which had two Serbian security guards, about 4 nautical miles off the coast of Somalia. European Naval Force Somalia Operation Atalanta also continues counter-piracy operations, which typically involve following captured vessels and mother ships. This is sometimes successful. When pirates boarded the Glamor , a merchant ship, in the Gulf of Aden in September, the crew locked themselves in their citadel, an armored safe room. The pirates fled after Operation Atalanta forces, the Indian Navy and a Japanese patrol aircraft responded. Illegal Fishing maritime piracy Somalia Share. somalia.summary: Recent reports indicate a resurgence of Somali piracy, particularly in the Gulf of Aden, with incidents increasing since April 2026. Although overall piracy rates are at their lowest in over three decades, the recent uptick highlights ongoing threats. The most significant incident involved the hijacking of the tanker Honour 25, resulting in casualties during a rescue attempt, marking the first pirate-related killings in over a decade. Contributing factors include the influence of Houthi rebels and illegal fishing, which has devastated local fishermen's livelihoods. As foreign trawlers deplete fish stocks, some locals have turned to piracy, exacerbating community tensions. In response, local authorities have restricted fishing activities, further straining food security. International efforts to combat piracy continue, with proposals for a new counter-piracy task force and ongoing operations by the European Naval Force. Analysts emphasize the importance of adhering to Best Management Practices to protect seafarers and vital trade routes.

Security Threats About ADF Contact Subscription Contribute Archive English Français العربية Português English Français العربية Português Home » Daily News » Signs of Peace Abound in Mogadishu Daily News Signs of Peace Abound in Mogadishu An al-Qaida-affiliated terror group has waged a 20-year insurgency in Somalia By ADF November 10, 2026 4 Mins Read Somali police patrol through central Mogadishu. GETTY IMAGES Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Email Reddit WhatsApp Copy Link Senior Somali officials say daily life in and around Mogadishu is gradually returning to normal amid the government’s 20-year battle against al-Shabaab. During a late September gathering of officials at the Ministry of Defense headquarters in Dayniile, Defense Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi noted the ability of senior officials to gather without fear of being attacked. Dayniile is a district about 8 kilometers north of Mogadishu, the national capital. “We remember four and a half years ago, when elections were being held here … mortar shells were raining down like stones around the hall where the election was taking place,” Fiqi said in a report by TRT Afrika. At the same gathering, Prime Minister Hamza Abdi Barre said he had travelled to the Defense Ministry from his residence without roads being closed for his convoy’s safety. “We simply moved among ordinary Somali citizens,” Barre said. “At certain points, we stopped. We were caught in traffic.” This might seem mundane, but for years senior officials in Mogadishu often traveled behind security cordons and armored vehicles on closed roads. TRT Afrika noted that Mogadishu now hosts large sporting events and cultural gatherings and that restaurants are staying open well after dark. During the 2026 World Cup, senior government officials were seen watching the matches with members of the public. During Independence Day Celebrations on July 1, President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud mingled with young people at Taleex Square — with a far less restrictive security presence. “These scenes are not simply evidence of improved security,” TRT Producer Nuri Aden wrote. “They are themselves part of the wider struggle against terrorism.” In other parts of the country, the al-Qaida-affiliated terror group maintains a persistent deadly presence. The terror group on October 26 attacked an estimated 2,000 members of the Somali National Army (SNA) and claimed they had killed 413 Soldiers and wounded 400 more. Somalia’s federal government did not disclose the number of SNA casualties but said more than 70 al-Shabaab fighters were killed. The SNA forces were attacked as they advanced toward the town of Burhakabo, where Ethiopian forces serving under the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) handed over a military base to the SNA in August. Al-Shabaab’s deadly resiliency fortifies the theory that an experienced, well-organized terror movement cannot be defeated by military force alone. Mohamud in September said the government also aims to confront the scourge ideologically and financially. Analysts say that positively engaging younger populations, especially underemployed young people in areas plagued by insecurity, can help governments stem the spread of radical thought. Al-Shabaab means “the youth,” and Somali officials are increasingly referring to the terror group as “Khawaarij,” after an extremist Islamic sect. Somalia’s government is portraying al-Shabaab as a movement that has twisted religion while attacking people it claims to defend. Authorities are also registering religious schools and Qur’anic study centers to bring Islamic education into a more cohesive national framework. As noted by TRT Afrika, a bill before parliament proposes the establishment of a Somali Scholars Council, a national body to unite religious scholars and help counter extremist religious interpretations. The council could promote religious awareness, support peace and reconciliation, improve social cohesion and counter the misuse of religion and extremist ideas, Minister of Endowments and Islamic Affairs Sheikh Mukhtar Robow Ali recently told lawmakers. Robow was once a senior al-Shabaab figure. Mogadishu has also begun targeting websites, social media outlets and online platforms used to promote terrorist propaganda. Military, security and police are working to prevent terrorists from controlling the narrative around security incidents. Authorities have also targeted financial accounts, communication channels and other systems believed to fund terror operations. Fiqi said in late September that security efforts have led to a precipitous drop in terror attacks in Mogadishu. He said in a TRT Afrika report that terrorist attacks have declined by 87%, and that the government aims to soon push the rate to beyond 90%. extremism national security Somali Terrorism Share. somalia.summary: In Mogadishu, signs of peace are emerging as daily life gradually normalizes amid the Somali government's ongoing battle against the al-Qaida-affiliated group al-Shabaab. Senior officials, including Defense Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi and Prime Minister Hamza Abdi Barre, have noted a significant reduction in security threats, allowing them to travel freely among citizens without heavy security measures. This shift is reflected in the resurgence of public events, such as sporting activities and cultural gatherings, which were previously hindered by violence. Despite these improvements, al-Shabaab remains a persistent threat, recently attacking Somali National Army forces and claiming significant casualties. The Somali government is addressing this challenge not only through military means but also by engaging youth and promoting a cohesive Islamic education framework. Efforts include establishing a Somali Scholars Council to counter extremist interpretations of Islam and targeting online platforms that spread terrorist propaganda. Overall, security efforts have reportedly led to an 87% decrease in attacks in Mogadishu.

somalia.title: U.S. maintains level 4 travel advisories for Uganda, DRC, Somalia and South Sudan - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: U.S. maintains level 4 travel advisories for Uganda, DRC, Somalia and South Sudan - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME SECURITY U.S. maintains level 4 travel advisories for Uganda, DRC, Somalia and South Sudan Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ by Timothy Cerullo Tuesday November 10, 2026 A collage of U.S. President Donald Trump and his Ugandan counterpart, Yoweri Museveni, during past separate events. Photo Trump/Museveni The United States government has issued its highest travel warning for four East African countries, including Uganda, urging its citizens and other foreigners to avoid visiting them because of security and health concerns. In a travel advisory issued on Monday, November 9, the U.S. Department of State placed Uganda, Somalia, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) under Level 4, the highest category in its four-level travel warning system. The four countries were flagged over terrorism, violent crime, kidnapping, political unrest and health risks, with the U.S. warning that its ability to provide emergency assistance to Americans in affected areas was limited. advertisements Uganda was specifically flagged over terrorism, armed robberies, home invasions, sexual assaults and the ongoing Ebola outbreak, which the U.S. government said had made it difficult to provide emergency assistance. The advisory also warned of possible terrorist attacks targeting religious institutions, schools, government buildings, police stations, transport centres and tourist attractions, particularly in major cities such as Kampala. On political stability, the U.S. warned that demonstrations could erupt without warning, especially during political events, adding that security officers had previously used tear gas, batons and rubber bullets against protesters. The U.S. government further raised concerns about Uganda's Anti-Homosexuality Act of 2023, which criminalises consensual same-sex relations and applies to both citizens and foreigners, with offenders facing life imprisonment. Somalia was also placed under Level 4 due to the risks of crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest, health concerns and landmines, with the U.S. government advising foreigners against travelling there for any reason. Other concerns raised by the U.S. included the systematic mistreatment of women and gay people, piracy, abuse of residents in rehabilitation centres and confiscation of passports by family members. The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) was also listed at Level 4 because of health concerns, crime, unrest, terrorism, and kidnapping, making it one of the countries foreigners have been advised to avoid. For Americans already in these countries, the U. S. government advised them to register with its Smart Traveller Enrollment Program (STEP) to receive security updates and make it easier for diplomatic officials to contact them during emergencies. President Donald Trump's administration also urged its citizens in the affected countries to avoid demonstrations, remain alert in public places, exercise caution when walking or driving at night and prepare emergency departure plans. Uganda, Somalia, South Sudan and the DRC join 22 other countries on the U.S. travel advisory system's Level 4 list, including Afghanistan, Belarus, Burkina Faso, Myanmar, the Central African Republic, Chad, Haiti, Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Libya, Mali, Niger, North Korea, Russia, Sudan, Syria, Ukraine and Yemen. "We issue Travel Advisories with Levels 1 to 4. Level 4 means do not travel. We assign Level 4 based on local conditions and our limited ability to help Americans there. These places are dangerous. Do not go for any reason," the U.S. government stated. The advisory, released on November 9, highlights concerns such as terrorism, violent crime, kidnapping, political unrest, and health threats, including an ongoing Ebola outbreak in Uganda. Specific warnings include potential terrorist attacks on public places and the risk of violent protests. Somalia faces similar dangers, including crime, terrorism, and systematic mistreatment of marginalized groups. The DRC is flagged for health issues and crime. The U.S. advises Americans in these regions to register with the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program for security updates and to prepare for emergencies. These countries join 22 others on the Level 4 list, emphasizing the serious risks associated with travel to these areas.

Dowladda Federaalka Galmudug Hiiraan News Jubaland News Koonfur Galbeed SSC Somaliland Follow us Search News Somalia US Forces Carry Out Overnight Airstrikes Against ISIS Positions in Somalia’s Puntland Region Posted by: Horseed Staff GAROWE, Somalia — US forces carried out a series of targeted airstrikes overnight in several areas of Qandala district in Somalia’s northeastern Bari region, targeting positions suspected of being used by Islamic State (ISIS) militants, according to field and security sources. 10 November, 2026 Share Tweet The strikes reportedly formed part of ongoing efforts to support military operations against the remaining ISIS elements operating in the strategically important Al-Miskad mountain range. The airstrikes focused primarily on the areas of Dabalyal and Halbaladi, as well as positions east of Dhadar, near strategic locations held by Puntland’s Darawiish forces in the vicinity of the Ja’il Sari valley. Security sources said the operation followed approximately four weeks of intelligence gathering and surveillance, which reportedly identified concentrations of ISIS operatives involved in coordinating field activities and planning the use of improvised explosive devices and landmines. Suspicious movements were also reportedly detected around Wangabli well and in the Gub and Gurdadin areas. Strategic Importance of the Ja’il Valley Security assessments indicate that ISIS fighters have maintained a significant presence along the eastern side of the Ja’il Valley, which has served as one of the group’s principal strongholds and operational centers. The area is believed to have hosted command facilities, medical installations and defensive positions used by the organization to coordinate its activities. The group has previously demonstrated its operational capabilities in the region. On September 27, ISIS militants reportedly launched an attack involving explosive-laden drones targeting the Dasan area. Earlier, on September 5, a landmine explosion between Shi’ab and Dhadar killed one of the group’s members. The latest US airstrikes follow a series of military operations conducted by Puntland’s Darawiish forces over the past two weeks on the western side of the Gacail Valley, covering areas between Daburad and Mirali. The western sector has previously been a significant battleground. In early 2025, an airstrike in the area reportedly killed ISIS’s head of foreign relations, an Iraqi national. Puntland forces also seized equipment and medical supplies in the Buqo Aliid and Ruq Ruq areas during operations in the Al-Miskad region. ISIS Presence and Concerns Over Regrouping ISIS has maintained a presence in Puntland since 2015, when a faction of Al-Shabaab fighters broke away from the group and pledged allegiance to ISIS rather than al-Qaeda. Since establishing its foothold in the region, the organization has carried out a series of bombings, targeted killings and other attacks. Security analysts have identified Puntland’s strategic location and difficult mountainous terrain as factors that have enabled the group to sustain its activities. ISIS has also reportedly strengthened its operational capacity through the recruitment of foreign fighters and financial resources obtained through extortion. Last year, the organization came close to establishing extensive control over parts of the Al-Miskad area, highlighting the security challenges facing Puntland authorities. Estimates by Puntland officials place the group’s strength at between 200 and 300 fighters, most of whom are reportedly from neighboring Ethiopia, alongside members of other nationalities. Recent movements in the eastern parts of the Gacail Valley have heightened concerns that ISIS is attempting to reorganize its forces, restore its operational networks and prepare for further attacks. Despite these concerns, Puntland’s Darawiish forces continue to maintain control over key corridors and strategic routes in the region. The latest airstrikes highlight the continuing military pressure on ISIS positions in northeastern Somalia and the importance of intelligence-led operations in preventing the group from rebuilding its presence in the Al-Miskad mountain range. somalia.summary: US forces conducted targeted airstrikes in Somalia's Puntland region, specifically in the Qandala district, against positions believed to be used by ISIS militants. The operation, which took place overnight, was part of ongoing efforts to dismantle ISIS's presence in the strategically significant Al-Miskad mountain range. The airstrikes focused on areas such as Dabalyal and Halbaladi, following four weeks of intelligence gathering that identified concentrations of ISIS operatives involved in planning attacks. Security assessments indicate that ISIS has maintained a stronghold in the Ja’il Valley, utilizing it for command and operational activities. Despite ongoing military pressure, including recent operations by Puntland's Darawiish forces, concerns remain about ISIS's ability to regroup and launch further attacks. The group, which has been active in Puntland since 2015, reportedly consists of 200 to 300 fighters, many of whom are foreign recruits. The airstrikes underscore the importance of intelligence-led operations in combating ISIS's resurgence in the region.

somalia.title: Türkiye and Somalia Discuss Security Cooperation Amid AU Peacekeeping Troop Withdrawal - Horseed Media
somalia.content: Türkiye and Somalia Discuss Security Cooperation Amid AU Peacekeeping Troop Withdrawal | Horseed Media Skip to content Search Home Somalia News Puntland News World News in English Featured More.. Dowladda Federaalka Galmudug Hiiraan News Jubaland News Koonfur Galbeed SSC Somaliland Follow us Search News Somalia Türkiye and Somalia Discuss Security Cooperation Amid AU Peacekeeping Troop Withdrawal Posted by: Horseed Staff MOGADISHU — Türkiye and Somalia have discussed military and security developments, counterterrorism efforts and bilateral cooperation as troop-contributing countries begin withdrawing forces from the African Union peacekeeping mission in Somalia. 10 November, 2026 Share Tweet Ferhat Alkan met Somalia’s National Security Adviser Awes Hagi Yusuf Ahmed in Mogadishu on November 9 2026. (Turkish Embassy in Somalia) The discussions took place during a meeting between Turkish Ambassador to Somalia Ferhat Alkan and Somalia’s National Security Adviser, Awes Hagi Yusuf Ahmed, in the Somali capital, Mogadishu. “Türkiye continues to contribute to the peace, stability, and security of Somalia, as it has in the past,” the Turkish Embassy said in a statement issued Tuesday. According to Somalia’s Office of the National Security Adviser, the meeting also addressed political developments, ongoing efforts to combat the Al Shabab terrorist group and broader areas of bilateral cooperation. During the talks, the Somali official expressed appreciation for Türkiye’s longstanding friendship and support, emphasizing the importance of continued coordination between the two countries to strengthen stability and security in Somalia. TURKSOM Mission Remains Central to Security Cooperation Türkiye’s military training mission in Somalia, known as TURKSOM, remains a key component of bilateral security cooperation and efforts to strengthen the capabilities of Somalia’s national security forces. The mission provides military training and logistical support to Somali troops as they continue operations against terrorist organizations, including Al Shabab and Daesh. Türkiye has maintained a significant role in supporting Somalia’s security institutions through military training, capacity-building initiatives and broader bilateral cooperation. The latest discussions underscore the continued importance of the Türkiye-Somalia partnership, particularly as Somalia navigates evolving security challenges and changes in the international peacekeeping presence in the country. somalia.summary: Türkiye and Somalia have engaged in discussions regarding military and security cooperation, particularly in light of the withdrawal of African Union peacekeeping troops from Somalia. The meeting took place on November 9, 2026, in Mogadishu between Turkish Ambassador Ferhat Alkan and Somalia’s National Security Adviser, Awes Hagi Yusuf Ahmed. The talks focused on counterterrorism efforts, political developments, and the ongoing fight against the Al Shabab terrorist group. The Turkish Embassy emphasized Türkiye's commitment to Somalia's peace and stability. A key aspect of their cooperation is the TURKSOM mission, which provides military training and logistical support to Somali forces. This partnership is crucial as Somalia faces evolving security challenges and adjusts to the changing international peacekeeping landscape. The discussions highlighted the importance of continued collaboration to enhance Somalia's security capabilities and ensure stability in the region.

somalia.summary: Somalia's former Chief Justice, Bashe Yusuf Ahmed, reported that over 300 security personnel have "militarily occupied" the Supreme Court following its ruling that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's term extension was unconstitutional. This occupation occurred after the court's decision, which challenged the legitimacy of the president's presidency. The situation highlights escalating tensions between the judiciary and the executive branch in Somalia, raising concerns about the rule of law and governance in the country. The military presence at the court underscores the precarious state of Somalia's political landscape, where judicial independence is threatened. The incident reflects broader issues of power struggles and the challenges faced in establishing a stable democratic framework in Somalia. As the situation develops, it remains to be seen how this will impact the country's political stability and the relationship between the government and its institutions.

football.summary: استعاد فريق الهلال السوداني لكرة القدم لقب الدوري الممتاز "النخبة" بعد قرار لجنة الاستئناف باتحاد الكرة، الذي صدر يوم الثلاثاء. كان الهلال قد فقد اللقب سابقًا لصالح غريمه المريخ، الذي اعتُبر فائزًا بمباراة القمة رغم خسارته في الملعب، بسبب عدم أهلية بعض اللاعبين المجنسين في صفوف الهلال. جاء قرار الاستئناف بعد تظلم الهلال، مما أدى إلى تراجع اللجنة عن قرارها السابق وإعادة اللقب إلى الهلال، الذي يمثل السودان في دوري أبطال إفريقيا. يُذكر أن الهلال قد حقق الفوز على المريخ بهدف اللاعب الليبيري إمانويل فلومو في نهائي بطولة "النخبة" الذي أقيم في 10 يونيو الماضي. وقد شهدت المرحلة الأخيرة من الدوري مشاركة ثمانية فرق بعد مرحلة أولى تضمنت 16 فريقًا موزعة على أربع مجموعات.

football.summary: استعاد الهلال السوداني لقب الدوري الممتاز بعد قرار لجنة الاستئنافات بالاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم، التي قبلت طلب المراجعة المقدم من النادي. القرار جاء بعد الجدل الذي أثاره منح نقاط مباراة القمة لغريمه التقليدي المريخ، حيث تم التراجع عن هذا القرار. الهلال أعلن عبر بيان رسمي أن اللجنة وافقت على طلبه من الناحيتين الشكلية والموضوعية، وألغت قرارها السابق الذي كان قد حول نقاط المباراة إلى المريخ. كما تم اعتماد نتيجة المباراة وفقًا لما ورد في تقرير حكم اللقاء. هذا القرار يعيد اللقب إلى خزائن الهلال، مما يعكس أهمية هذه القضية في الساحة الرياضية السودانية. يعتبر هذا التطور نقطة تحول في المنافسة بين الأندية الكبرى في السودان، ويعزز من مكانة الهلال في تاريخ الدوري الممتاز.

football.summary: استعاد الهلال السوداني رسميًا لقب الدوري الممتاز بعد قرار لجنة الاستئنافات بالاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم. جاء ذلك بعد قبول طلب المراجعة الذي تقدم به النادي، حيث تراجعت اللجنة عن قرارها السابق الذي منح غريمه التقليدي المريخ نقاط مباراة القمة. وأكد الهلال في بيان رسمي أن اللجنة وافقت على طلبه من الناحيتين الشكلية والموضوعية، مما أدى إلى إلغاء قرار تحويل النقاط إلى المريخ واعتماد نتيجة المباراة كما وردت في تقرير الحكم. تم اتخاذ هذا القرار بعد اجتماعين للجنة يومي 9 و10 نوفمبر، برئاسة محمد البشير. يُعتبر هذا القرار تأكيدًا لمكانة الهلال في تاريخ كرة القدم السودانية، حيث يُعد من أبرز الأندية وأكثرها تتويجًا بالبطولات المحلية. وبذلك، ينتهي الجدل حول هوية بطل المسابقة ويستعيد الهلال صدارة المشهد.
